title: Study on Creative AI Applied Genetic Algorithm
content: Large language model (LLM)-based creative AI systems can already automate much of the research cycle—from literature survey and hypothesis generation to experimentation and manuscript writing—yet they remain limited in producing genuinely novel ideas, since LLMs primarily generate the statistically most plausible continuation of existing text. This study proposes a creative AI model that applies a genetic algorithm (GA) to explore combinations of Method, Problem, and Goal elements drawn from a knowledge space built from existing papers, aiming to generate research-theme hypotheses with higher novelty than LLM-only approaches. Candidate hypotheses are represented as individuals and evolved through elitism, crossover, and mutation, guided by a fitness function that combines novelty and utility scores; the top-scoring hypothesis is then re-evaluated for novelty and utility before being used to auto-generate a manuscript draft. Three manuscript-generation conditions, sharing the same eight-section structure and evaluated under four criteria (Originality, Quality, Reproducibility, Significance) adapted from major AI conference review guidelines, were compared: (A) the proposed model writing the manuscript end-to-end on its own, via its genetic-algorithm hypothesis search together with a locally hosted LLM writer, with no external agent and no live web access; (B) the same genetic-algorithm-selected hypothesis handed to an existing AI agent (Google Gemini Deep Research) for writing; and (C) the same AI agent writing entirely on its own, with no genetic-algorithm involvement. Within the scope of the evaluated cases, Condition (A) achieved the highest overall score, driven by higher Quality and Significance rather than by Originality: comparing (B) against (C) with the writing agent held constant showed a clear genetic-algorithm-driven gain in Quality and Significance, and this gain persisted even when (A) used a less capable writer than (C). Originality itself did not distinguish (A) from (C) in this experiment—both scored at the ceiling of the present instrument, a resolution limitation of the small reference knowledge space used here rather than evidence against genetic-algorithm-based novelty, and is discussed as an open question for future work.
